entries.definition: the four transaction guarantees: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
a translation layer (or pattern) that makes two incompatible interfaces work together without changing either.
in DDD, a cluster of objects treated as a single consistency and persistence unit, entered only through its root.
Additive Increase / Multiplicative Decrease, TCP's rule of growing the window slowly and halving it on loss.
speeding up one part of a program can never gain more than that part's share of total runtime.
the average cost per operation over many operations, even if a few individual ones are expensive (e.g. dynamic-array append).
announcing the same IP from many locations so the network routes each client to the nearest healthy site.
vector search that trades a little recall for big speed when finding similar embeddings.
a translation boundary that stops an external or legacy model from leaking into your domain.
a single edge front door centralizing auth, rate limiting, TLS termination, and routing for inbound traffic.
a system that favors availability over consistency during a network partition (serves possibly-stale data).
compiling fully to native machine code before the program runs, the opposite of JIT.
a transaction either fully completes or has no effect at all.
a tree representation of source code that encodes nesting and operator precedence.
the transformer mechanism that weighs how much each token should focus on every other token.
the probability a classifier ranks a random positive example above a random negative one.
the fraction of time a system is up and serving correctly, usually measured in "nines".
an isolated data center within a cloud region with its own power and cooling.
a self-balancing binary search tree where sibling subtree heights differ by at most one.
slowing producers (or bounding buffers) when consumers fall behind, instead of crashing or dropping data.
recursion over a tree of choices that undoes each choice to try alternatives ("choose, explore, un-choose").
the loose alternative to ACID: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency.
a TCP congestion-control algorithm that models bottleneck bandwidth and RTT instead of reacting to packet loss.
deliberately slow, memory-hard password-hashing functions that make brute force infeasible.
a shortest-path algorithm that handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles.
a gateway tailored to one client type (e.g. a separate mobile and web BFF).
an upper bound on how an algorithm's work grows as input size grows.
a complete binary tree (stored in an array) where each parent out-ranks its children; backs priority queues.
repeatedly halving a sorted range to find a target in O(log n).
an incident writeup that fixes the system that allowed the failure rather than punishing a person.
raw fixed-size addressable disk blocks attached to one host; lowest latency, used for DB files and VM disks.
a compact probabilistic set that says "definitely not present" or "probably present", with no false negatives.
running two full environments and flipping all traffic at once, giving instant rollback at double cost.
"Bottom Line Up Front", putting the conclusion or ask in the first sentence of a doc.
a search ranking function that improves on TF-IDF with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalization.
Boyce-Codd Normal Form, a normalization rule stricter than 3NF requiring every functional dependency's left side to be a superkey.
a boundary within which a domain model and its terms have one consistent meaning; the unit for service boundaries.
a balanced, high-fan-out tree with sorted leaves that backs almost all relational database indexes.
a region of RAM that caches recently-used database pages to avoid disk I/O.
isolating resources (e.g. a thread pool per dependency) so one saturated dependency can't starve the others.
how fast you are consuming your error budget relative to the SLO window.
how many people can be lost before a project stalls; code review raises it.
a compact instruction set for a virtual machine, sitting between source code and native machine code.
the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and populates the cache itself.
many requests miss the same expired hot key at once and all rebuild it from the database simultaneously.
routing a small traffic slice to a new version and widening only if metrics stay healthy.

too many unique metric label combinations (e.g. per-user labels) creating millions of time series.
one slow service causing callers' threads to pile up, propagating slowness until healthy services also fail.
an atomic instruction that updates memory only if it still holds an expected value.
tailing a database's write-ahead log to publish committed row changes downstream.
a global network of edge caches that serve content near users to cut latency.
a leaf certificate signed by an intermediate CA, signed up to a root CA the client already trusts.
a Linux kernel feature that limits what a process can *use* (CPU, memory, I/O); a building block of containers.
the point where a database flushes dirty pages to disk, or where a stream engine snapshots state for recovery.
deliberately failing production components to prove the system is resilient.
a saga style where services react to events with no central coordinator (vs orchestration).
IP address notation where /N means the first N bits are the network portion (e.g. /24 = 256 addresses).
a resilience pattern that trips after failures and fails fast for a cooldown to stop cascading failures.
a design where source-code dependencies all point inward toward business rules.
an index whose leaves store the full rows in key order, so the index *is* the table.
how focused a single module is on one job; you want it high.
the LSM-tree background merge that drops dead data and bounds read/space amplification.
a step that semantically undoes a prior committed local transaction in a saga (e.g. a refund).
a tree where every level is full except possibly the last, which fills left to right.
preferring "has-a" plug-in behavior over deep "is-a" class hierarchies.
TCP's mechanism protecting the shared network via the congestion window (vs flow control).
placing nodes and keys on a ring so adding/removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys.
a normal Linux process isolated by namespaces and constrained by cgroups, sharing the host kernel.
saving one thread's CPU state and restoring another's so the CPU can run a different thread.
automatically building and testing every small change against main, many times a day.
a system's design ends up mirroring the communication structure of the org that builds it.
sharing pages read-only and copying only when one side writes, making operations like fork cheap.
a probabilistic structure estimating item frequencies in fixed memory (only overcounts).
how much one module depends on another; you want it low.
an index containing every column a query needs, so the query is answered without touching the table.
a system that favors consistency over availability during a partition (refuses possibly-stale answers).
Command Query Responsibility Segregation, separating the write model from denormalized read models.
a fast non-cryptographic checksum for detecting accidental data corruption.
a Conflict-free Replicated Data Type whose merges converge automatically without coordination.
a region of code that at most one thread may execute at a time.
a Kubernetes pod state where a container keeps crashing and restarting.
Cross-Site Request Forgery, tricking a logged-in browser into making an unwanted authenticated request.
a membership filter that, unlike a Bloom filter, supports deletion and is often more space-efficient.
fetching rows after a given sort-key position, giving stable O(limit) pages.
a directed graph with no cycles; used for dependencies, build order, and query plans.
a separate destination for messages that fail after capped retries, keeping the main flow unblocked.
a cycle of transactions or threads each waiting on a resource the others hold.
a pattern that adds behavior to an object dynamically by wrapping it, without subclassing.
layering independent security controls so no single failure is catastrophic.
deliberately duplicating pre-joined data to speed reads, at the cost of write complexity.
a controller managing identical stateless pod replicas with rolling updates and rollbacks.
a trick to apply many range updates cheaply, then prefix-sum once to get final values.
a greedy shortest-path algorithm for non-negative edge weights using a min-priority-queue.
depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete classes.
services that deploy in lockstep or share a database, paying microservice costs with no benefit.
the system translating human-readable names into IP addresses via a cached, hierarchical lookup.
the four delivery metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, change-failure rate, and MTTR.
append-only balanced debits and credits where balances are derived by summing, never overwritten.

writing to a database and a broker non-atomically, risking inconsistency if a crash happens between.
once a transaction commits, its effects survive crashes.
solving each overlapping subproblem once and caching the result ("recursion plus reuse").
99.999999999% durability, meaning essentially never losing a stored object.
Extract, Load, Transform: load raw data into the warehouse first, then transform it there (vs ETL).
a vector of numbers representing meaning, where similar meanings sit close together.
bundling data with the only code allowed to change it, hidden behind a small public interface.
the average information per symbol from a source; the hard lower bound for lossless compression.
splitting data into k data plus m parity shards to survive m losses at low storage overhead.
100% minus the SLO; the amount of unreliability you are allowed to spend before freezing releases.
a consistent distributed key-value store (using Raft) holding all Kubernetes cluster state.
single-threaded concurrency for I/O-bound work, juggling many waits without locks.
storing an append-only log of events as the source of truth, deriving current state by replay.

increasing the wait between retries to give a struggling service room to recover.
adding new schema without removing old, migrating in steps, then removing old later.
a pattern hiding a complex subsystem behind one simple front-door interface.
when a control (e.g. a rate limiter store) is down, fail-open keeps availability, fail-closed keeps protection.
two cores updating different variables on the same cache line, causing it to ping-pong between caches.
pushing content to followers at write time (cheap reads) vs merging at read time (cheap writes).
two pointers moving at different speeds, used for cycle detection and finding the middle of a list.
a runtime switch that turns code paths on or off, decoupling deploy from release.
a monotonically increasing ID given to each new leader; storage rejects writes with a stale token.
making cloud cost visible and owned by engineers rather than a finance surprise.
a profiling visualization where box width is total time spent; scan for the widest leaf to find the hot path.
a test that passes and fails without code changes, usually from non-determinism.
proof that in a fully asynchronous system where one node may crash, no algorithm can guarantee consensus always terminates.
TCP's mechanism protecting the receiver via its advertised receive window (vs congestion control).
past sessions stay safe even if the long-term private key later leaks (provided by ephemeral key exchange).
X→Y means any rows agreeing on X must agree on Y; the basis of normalization.
automatic reclamation of unreachable heap memory, typically via tracing from roots.
a metric that goes up and down, read instantaneously (e.g. memory usage, queue depth).
directly reachable references (stack variables, registers, globals) from which a tracing collector starts.
the observation that most objects die young, motivating young/old GC generations.
peer-to-peer rumor spreading where info reaches all N nodes in about O(log N) rounds.
serving a simpler or cached response when a dependency is down, so the core flow still works.
a query language letting clients request exactly the fields they need in one round trip.
building a solution by always taking the locally best choice and never reconsidering.
a high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 transport and binary Protobuf encoding.
a compressor combining LZ77 (remove repeats) with Huffman entropy coding.
a guarantee that one action's effects are visible to another, established by locks, atomics, or thread joins.
building a hash table on the smaller input and probing with the larger; best for big unsorted equality joins.
an array plus a hash function mapping keys to slots, giving average O(1) lookup, insert, and delete.
the Hadoop Distributed File System, storing large files in big replicated blocks (default 128 MB).
one stalled item blocking everything behind it (e.g. a lost TCP packet stalling all streams).
the region for dynamically-sized or long-lived data; must be managed manually or by a GC.
sending a duplicate request to another replica after a delay and taking the first reply, to cut tail latency.
a metric recording a distribution into buckets so you can compute percentiles like p95/p99.
adding more machines and spreading load across them (vs vertical scaling).
one key or shard taking disproportionate traffic, often from bad or monotonic keys.

multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, fixing application-layer head-of-line blocking.
runs over QUIC on UDP with independent per-stream loss recovery, fixing transport head-of-line blocking.
assigning short codes to frequent symbols and long codes to rare ones for compression.
a probabilistic structure estimating the count of distinct items in tiny memory.

Identity and Access Management, controlling who can do what in a cloud, ideally with least privilege.
a property where doing an operation many times has the same effect as doing it once (safe to retry).
a client-supplied unique token letting the server dedupe retries and apply an operation exactly once.
Inverse Document Frequency, a search-ranking weight that boosts rare terms and discounts common ones.
an auxiliary structure (usually a B+tree) that speeds lookups at the cost of extra writes and space.
describing infrastructure in version-controlled declarative files for reproducible setups.
HTTP/HTTPS routing from outside the cluster with host/path rules and TLS termination.
a map from each term to the list of documents that contain it; the core of full-text search.
the set of Kafka replicas currently caught up to the leader and eligible for election.
transactions appear to run as if alone; isolation levels trade safety for concurrency.
interpreting first, then compiling hot code to native machine code at runtime guided by profiling.
combining rows from two tables on a matching condition (a Cartesian product plus a selection).
a signed JSON token (header, payload, signature) that is tamper-proof but, by default, only signed not encrypted.
finding the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in O(n) with a running sum that resets when negative.
a distributed append-only log for high-volume, replayable event streams, partitioned for parallelism.
topological sort by repeatedly outputting in-degree-zero vertices.
treating everything as a stream, with batch as the finite special case, avoiding dual codebases.
"Keep It Simple": prefer the simplest design that works.
the Knuth-Morris-Pratt string-matching algorithm, linear-time via a precomputed failure function.
a system that runs containers across many machines and continuously reconciles toward your declared state.
see Q.
lake-priced object storage plus ACID transactions via a table format like Iceberg or Delta.
a logical counter guaranteeing that if A happened-before B then LC(A) < LC(B), but it cannot detect concurrency.
the time to complete one request, best reported as percentiles (p99) not averages.
one leader takes all writes and replicates to read-serving followers.
any replica accepts writes and quorums reconcile (Dynamo/Cassandra style).
a load-balancing algorithm routing to the backend with the fewest active connections.

a sequence of nodes each pointing to the next; O(1) insert/delete at a known node but O(n) indexing.

a component spreading requests across backends behind one address and removing unhealthy ones.
proactively rejecting requests (least-important first) when overloaded, returning 503.
the tendency to reuse recent addresses (temporal) or nearby ones (spatial), why caches work.
a primitive enforcing that only one thread runs a critical section at a time.
a router forwarding using the most specific matching prefix in its table.
an eviction policy that discards the entry untouched for the longest time.
an eviction policy that discards the least-frequently-accessed entry.
a write-optimized engine appending to a memtable, flushing sorted SSTables, and compacting later.
a subtype must be usable anywhere its parent is, with no surprises.
a compression technique replacing repeats with back-references of length and distance.
a tracing GC that marks reachable objects from roots, then sweeps the unmarked as garbage.
a formula for solving divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n).
an abstract structure whose exchange axiom guarantees a greedy algorithm finds the optimum.
a batch model of a parallel map step, a network shuffle by key, and a reduce aggregation.
writing code that respects how the CPU and memory actually work, to get more performance.
top-down recursion with a cache storing each subproblem result the first time it is computed.
an instruction forbidding reordering across it and flushing buffered writes so other cores see them.
the in-RAM sorted write buffer of an LSM tree that flushes to an SSTable when full.
splitting a system into many independently deployed services that talk over the network.
a heap whose root is always the smallest / largest element.
the Memory Management Unit that translates virtual addresses to physical ones using page tables.
one codebase built and deployed as a single unit, with in-process communication.
a stack kept strictly increasing or decreasing, solving "next greater element" in O(n).
the cheapest set of edges connecting all nodes with no cycle (built by Kruskal or Prim).

injecting small bugs into code to check whether the test suite catches them.
keeping multiple row versions so readers read old committed versions while writers create new ones.

provisioning enough capacity to lose one failure domain and still meet the SLO.
a kernel feature limiting what a process can *see* (PIDs, network, mounts); a building block of containers.

for each outer row, scanning the inner table; best when one side is tiny or selectively indexed.
layers of weighted sums plus nonlinearities that learn their own features from data.
a co-located workload stealing CPU, cache, or I/O and inflating your tail latency.
organizing tables to remove redundancy and update/insert/delete anomalies.

a protocol for delegated authorization, letting an app act on your behalf without your password.

the ability to ask new questions about a system's internal state from its outputs (logs, metrics, traces).

the Open Container Initiative standard for image format, runtime behavior, and registry distribution.
